subject: Anatomy
question_text: Identify the structure marked in the image below.

explanation.text:
The structure marked is the lacunar ligament.

Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament is a thick triangular band of tissue formed from fibres of the medial end of the inguinal ligament and fascia lata. It forms the medial wall of the femoral canal, and the apex of the triangle is attached to the pubic tubercle.

The inguinal (Poupart's) ligament is the thickened external oblique aponeurosis stretched between the ASIS and pubic tubercle. The pectineal (Astley-Cooper's) ligament is a strong fibrous band extending laterally along the pectineal line from the pectineal attachment of the lacunar ligament. The conjoint tendon is formed by the common aponeurosis of internal oblique and transversus abdominis and inserts into the pubic crest/pectineal line.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: Which of the following statements is true about the iliopubic tract?

options.label: a
options.text: It is a thickening of the lumbar fascia

options.label: b
options.text: It lies anterior to the Poupart's ligament

options.label: c
options.text: It inserts into the pubic tubercle in front of the conjoint tendon

options.label: d
options.text: Its fibers fan out with fascia iliaca laterally

correct_answer_text: Its fibers fan out with fascia iliaca laterally

explanation.text:
The fibres of the iliopubic tract fan out with fascia iliaca laterally.

The iliopubic tract is a thickening of the transversalis fascia lying immediately posterior to the inguinal (Poupart's) ligament. It extends from the ASIS superolaterally and arches across the front of the femoral sheath.

Medially, its fibres insert broadly into the pubic tubercle and pectineal line behind the conjoint tendon. Laterally, its fibres fan out within the transversalis fascia and fascia iliaca without bony attachment to the iliac spines.

Clinical note: it is an important landmark in laparoscopic hernia surgery.

question_text: Which of the following does not form the bony pelvis?

explanation.text:
The L5 lumbar vertebra does not form the bony pelvis.

The bony pelvis consists of two hip bones, the sacrum, and the coccyx. Their articulations form two sacroiliac joints, the sacrococcygeal symphysis, and the pubic symphysis.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: A 33-year-old primigravida presented at term with non-engagement of the fetal head. She is suspected to have cephalopelvic disproportion at the level of inlet. Which of the following does not form the boundary of the involved structure?

explanation.text:
The structure involved in cephalopelvic disproportion at the level of the inlet is the pelvic inlet. The ischial tuberosity does not form a boundary of the pelvic inlet.

Boundaries of the pelvic inlet: posteriorly the sacral promontory; laterally the arcuate line on the medial surface of the ilium and the pectineal line on the superior pubic ramus; anteriorly the pubic symphysis.

Boundaries of the pelvic outlet: posteriorly the tip of the coccyx; laterally the ischial tuberosities and inferior margin of the sacrotuberous ligament; anteriorly the pubic arch.

Clinical significance: cephalopelvic disproportion can occur when inlet or outlet diameters are shortened enough to prevent engagement of the fetal head.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: A patient with sciatica was found to have inflammation of the muscle marked below. Identify it.

explanation.text:
The marked muscle is the piriformis muscle.

Origin: anterior surface of sacrum, posterior inferior iliac spine, capsule of sacroiliac joint, and sacrotuberous ligament. Insertion: greater trochanter of femur. Action: lateral rotation of the thigh in extension and abduction of the thigh in the flexed position.

Piriformis forms the posterolateral wall of the pelvic cavity. The sciatic nerve is closely related and may pass through its fibres or below the muscle.

Clinical significance: piriformis syndrome is compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis, often associated with pain along the sciatic distribution (sciatica).

subject: Anatomy
question_text: Which of the following is false about the levator ani?

options.label: a
options.text: Contraction leads to occlusion of the vaginal canal

options.label: b
options.text: Puborectalis and pubococcygeus create the anorectal angle

options.label: d
options.text: Arises from the condensation of the piriformis fascia

correct_answer_text: Arises from the condensation of the piriformis fascia

explanation.text:
The levator ani arises from a condensation of obturator fascia forming the tendinous arch of levator ani, not from piriformis fascia.

The vaginal, urethral, and rectal hiatuses are occluded by contraction of levator ani and relaxation is needed for defecation and urination. Pubococcygeus and puborectalis help maintain rectal tone and create the anorectal angle.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: During the evaluation of a patient with erectile dysfunction, his internal pudendal artery was found to be stenosed. Which of the following vessels is this a branch of?

options.label: a
options.text: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

options.label: b
options.text: Posterior division of internal iliac artery

correct_answer_text: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

explanation.text:
The anterior division of the internal iliac artery gives rise to the internal pudendal artery.

The internal iliac artery divides at the superior border of the greater sciatic foramen into anterior and posterior trunks.

Anterior-trunk branches listed in the source include obturator, superior vesical, inferior vesical, inferior gluteal, middle rectal, vaginal (female), uterine (female), and internal pudendal arteries. Posterior-trunk branches include iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: While examining a patient with a direct inguinal hernia, you note that the sac protrudes through Hesselbach's triangle. Where does the structure forming its lateral boundary originate from?

options.label: a
options.text: Anterior trunk of the internal iliac artery

options.label: b
options.text: Posterior trunk of the internal iliac artery

explanation.text:
The lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle is formed by the inferior epigastric artery, which originates from the external iliac artery.

Branches of the external iliac artery include the deep circumflex iliac and inferior epigastric arteries, small branches to psoas major and nearby lymph nodes, and continuation as the femoral artery.

Clinical significance: the inferior epigastric artery contributes to the corona mortis; injury in this region can cause severe hemorrhage.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: Which of the following is a tributary of the common iliac vein?

explanation.text:
The median sacral vein is a tributary of the common iliac vein.

Tributaries of the common iliac vein include median sacral, iliolumbar, and occasionally lateral sacral veins. Internal iliac tributaries include superior and inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, obturator, lateral sacral, middle rectal, vesical, and uterine/vaginal veins. External iliac tributaries include inferior epigastric, deep circumflex iliac, and pubic veins.

Clinical note: agenesis of the external iliac vein has been reported in association with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome.

question_text: Which of the following does not form an anatomical boundary of the perineum?

explanation.text:
The sacrospinous ligament does not form an anatomical boundary of the perineum.

The perineum is a diamond-shaped region overlying the pelvic outlet. Its boundaries are: anteriorly the pubic symphysis and arcuate ligament; posteriorly the coccyx; anterolaterally the ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities; posterolaterally the sacrotuberous ligaments.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: A line between which of the following structures divides the perineum into anterior and posterior triangles?

explanation.text:
An imaginary line joining the two ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into an anterior urogenital triangle and a posterior anal/anogenital triangle.

The urogenital triangle faces downwards and forwards. In males it contains the scrotum and root of the penis; in females, the mons pubis and labia with the vestibule. The anal triangle faces downwards and backwards and contains the anal canal with its sphincters and the ischioanal fossae.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: A 30-year-old man with a history of blunt trauma to the pelvis was diagnosed with urethral rupture. Imaging revealed extravasation of the urine into the superficial perineal pouch. The attachment of which of the following fascia prevents extravasation into the thigh and anal triangle?

explanation.text:
Colles' fascia prevents extravasated urine from spreading into the thigh and anal triangle.

Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the superficial fascia of the scrotum and becomes Colles' fascia in the perineum. In women it continues into the labia majora and perineal fascia.

Colles' fascia attaches posteriorly to the perineal membrane, preventing fluid spread into the anal triangle, and laterally to the ischiopubic rami and fascia lata along Holden's line, preventing spread into the thigh.

Camper's fascia is the superficial fatty layer of abdominal superficial fascia; Scarpa's fascia is its deep membranous layer; Buck's fascia is the deep fascia of the penis.

Clinical significance: with urethral rupture, urine may extravasate into the superficial perineal pouch, penis, scrotum/labia majora, and anterior abdominal wall.

question_text: Which of the following is not a content of the superficial perineal pouch?

explanation.text:
Bulbourethral glands are not a content of the superficial perineal pouch; they are in the deep perineal pouch.

The superficial perineal pouch is the potential space between the perineal membrane above and Colles' fascia below. Its contents differ in males and females and include the roots of the external genitalia, superficial perineal muscles, and related neurovascular structures.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: Which of the following muscles is not involved in the formation of the perineal body?

explanation.text:
The internal anal sphincter is not involved in formation of the perineal body.

The perineal body is a fibromuscular structure in the midline at the junction of the anal and urogenital triangles. Muscular attachments include anteriorly superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles and bulbospongiosus; posteriorly the external anal sphincter; superiorly puborectalis, pubovaginalis, and the rectovaginal septum.

It is continuous with the perineal membrane and superficial perineal fascia. In males it continues as the perineal raphe; in females it attaches to the posterior commissure and introitus.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: A surgeon is dissecting the ischioanal fossa in a patient with anal cancer. Which of the following statements is correct about its boundaries?

options.label: a
options.text: Posterior boundary is the perineal membrane

options.label: b
options.text: Anterior boundary is the sacrotuberous ligament

options.label: c
options.text: Lateral boundary is the obturator internus

options.label: d
options.text: Medial boundary is the gluteus maximus

correct_answer_text: Lateral boundary is the obturator internus

explanation.text:
The lateral boundary of the ischioanal fossa is formed by obturator internus with its fascia.

The ischioanal fossa is a wedge-shaped fat-filled space on either side of the anal canal. Boundaries: anterior — posterior border of perineal membrane; posterior — gluteus maximus and sacrotuberous ligament; lateral — ischial tuberosity and obturator internus; medial — external anal sphincter and pelvic diaphragm (levator ani).

Clinical significance: the ischioanal fossa provides a relatively bloodless surgical plane during resection of anal cancers.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: The fascia of which of the following muscles is involved in the formation of the Alcock's canal?

explanation.text:
Alcock's (pudendal) canal is formed by the fascia of the obturator internus muscle.

It is created by connective tissue binding the internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve to the medial surface of obturator internus fascia.

Contents: internal pudendal artery and pudendal nerve.

Clinical significance: pudendal nerve block at the ischial spine can provide analgesia to the lower vagina, posterior perineum, and vulva; pudendal neuralgia may result from nerve compression in the canal.
